content: A chevron plot is a graphical representation used to analyze the kinetics of protein folding in the presence of varying concentrations of a denaturant. Denaturants are chemical agents that disrupt the native tertiary structure of proteins. The plot is referred to as a chevron plot because it typically exhibits a V-shaped or chevron-like appearance when the logarithm of the observed relaxation rate is plotted against the concentration of the denaturant. In a system that follows a two-state folding mechanism, the folding and unfolding rates dominate the observed relaxation rates below and above the denaturation midpoint (Cm), respectively. This characteristic gives rise to the terms folding arm and unfolding arm to describe the two limbs of the chevron plot. The denaturation midpoint (Cm) of a protein can be determined from equilibrium experiments prior to kinetic analysis. When fitting the data to a two-state model, it is assumed that the logarithms of the folding and unfolding rates vary linearly with the concentration of the denaturant. The slopes of these linear relationships are referred to as the folding m-value (mf) and the unfolding m-value (mu), collectively known as the kinetic m-values. The observed relaxation rate is the sum of the folding and unfolding rates. A strong agreement between the equilibrium m-value and the absolute sum of the kinetic m-values is generally considered evidence of two-state folding behavior. Most denaturation experiments are conducted at 298 K, with urea or guanidinium chloride (GuHCl) commonly used as denaturants. To generate the folding arm of the chevron plot, the protein is initially dissolved in a highly concentrated denaturant solution. This solution is then rapidly diluted (within less than a millisecond) into a buffer to achieve a specific final denaturant concentration. This process is typically performed using a stopped-flow apparatus. The relaxation of the protein to its new equilibrium state is monitored using spectroscopic techniques, such as fluorescence or, less commonly, circular dichroism (CD). The final protein concentration in the mixture is usually maintained between 1 and 20 µM, depending on the signal-to-noise ratio and the amplitude of the relaxation signal. The unfolding arm of the chevron plot is generated in a similar manner. In this case, a denaturant-free protein solution is mixed with a concentrated denaturant solution in buffer. When the logarithm of the relaxation rates obtained from these experiments is plotted against the final denaturant concentration, the resulting graph is the chevron plot. The mixing process determines the dead time of the instrument, which is typically around one millisecond. Therefore, a stopped-flow apparatus is suitable only for proteins with relaxation times on the order of a few milliseconds. For proteins with relaxation times shorter than the instrument's dead time, the experimental temperature can be lowered to increase the viscosity of the solution, thereby slowing the relaxation process to a measurable timescale. For fast-folding proteins with relaxation rates in the range of 1–100 microseconds, alternative techniques such as temperature-jump (T-jump, with a dead time of a few nanoseconds) or continuous flow mixing (with a dead time of a few microseconds) can be employed to generate chevron plots at different denaturant concentrations. Although the limbs of a chevron plot are generally assumed to exhibit linear dependence on denaturant concentration, deviations from linearity, known as chevron roll-overs, are sometimes observed. These roll-overs can occur in one or both limbs of the plot. The underlying causes of chevron roll-overs are not fully understood, but several hypotheses have been proposed. These include the presence of on-pathway folding intermediates, limitations imposed by the dead time of the instrument, shifts in the transition state (Hammond effect), protein aggregation artifacts, downhill folding, and salt-induced Debye-Hückel effects. In many cases, roll-overs in the folding arm are ignored because they occur at low denaturant concentrations. The data is then fit to a two-state model with a linear dependence of the rates on denaturant concentration. However, this approach can lead to an overestimation of the folding rates for such proteins in the absence of denaturants.
